items.title: Delegating decision authority to AI in recruitment: an empirical study of trust, control and algorithmic accountability
items.abstract: Purpose The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource (HR) practices has led to a growing number of organizations trying to understand the use of AI in recruitment. While AI is increasingly embedded in HR practices, few studies focus on how trust in AI is formed and how it shapes the adoption of AI in recruitment. Design/methodology/approach This study employed a qualitative research design based on 21 semi-structured interviews with HR professionals working in large, internationally operating German family-owned organizations that use AI in recruitment. The data was analysed using a theory-guided qualitative approach following the Gioia methodology to construct a systematic data structure linking participants’ experiences to established theoretical dimensions of trust. Findings The findings reveal that trust in AI is shaped by three interrelated dimensions: ability, integrity and benevolence. The study underscores how trust serves as a dynamic slider that governs the degree of decision authority delegated to AI systems, varying from automated screening for habitual tasks to human oversight for complex, cognitive tasks. Key tensions also emerge around power, control and trust breakdown. Practical implications First, the study emphasizes that organizations should recognize that successful AI adoption depends not only on technical performance, but also on deliberate trust-building strategies. By investing in transparency mechanisms, such as explainable AI interfaces, organizations can get a clear understanding of how recruitment algorithms operate. Second, organizations should invest in structured training programs to develop the efficiency and confidence of HR professionals working with AI systems. This can be done by offering training that focusses on interpreting algorithmic outputs, recognizing potential biases and maintaining ethical oversight. Third, organizations should establish formal governance frameworks that define accountability, certification standards and internal usage guidelines, which can reduce uncertainty and promote consistent, responsible AI practices in recruitment practices. Originality/value The study contributes to the technology acceptance model (TAM) and the algorithmic accountability theory by demonstrating how trust conditions the adoption of AI in recruitment. It theorizes how micro-level trust judgements are structurally conditioned by macro-level institutional safeguards and provides empirical insights into how HR professionals balance human judgement and algorithmic decision-making.

items.title: Design and Implementation of a Telegram-Based Conversational AI Agent for Automated Personal Expense Management Using Large Language Models and Google Sheets
items.abstract: Manual logging of day-to-day personal expenses is often abandoned by users because it requires them to open a dedicated spreadsheet or application and enter data in a rigid, structured format. This paper presents the design and implementation of a conversational Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent that allows a user to record and retrieve personal expenses simply by chatting in natural language through the Telegram messaging platform. The system is built using the n8n low-code automation platform and combines a Telegram Trigger node, an AI Agent powered by an OpenAI Chat Model, a Simple Memory module for conversational context, and two Google Sheets tools, namely Read Expenses and Add Expense, that allow the agent to write new expense records to, and retrieve existing records from, a connected Google Sheet. When a user sends a message such as "I spent Rs.231 for Medicine today," the agent extracts the expense description, amount, and date, appends the entry to the spreadsheet, and returns a natural-language confirmation. The agent can also generate an on-demand categorized daily summary. The proposed system was implemented and tested with real conversational data, and the results demonstrate that the agent accurately parses free-form expense statements, updates the backend spreadsheet correctly, and produces coherent, human-readable summaries, thereby lowering the friction traditionally associated with manual expense tracking.

items.abstract: Mobility as a Service (MaaS) offers a promising framework for promoting sustainable travel by integrating multiple transport modes and services into a single digital platform. This chapter explores how MaaS interfaces can be designed to support behaviour change towards more sustainable mobility choices using a combined approach that integrates systems thinking with user-centred design. Recognising MaaS as a complex sociotechnical system, this chapter applies cognitive work analysis (CWA) within the User-Centred Ecological Interface Design (UCEID) methodology to systematically examine the constraints that shape user decision-making and behaviour. By focusing on users’ interactions with a MaaS interface throughout journey planning, execution, navigation, and completion, this chapter offers tailored insights to support behaviour change towards sustainable travel. Key areas for consideration include enhancing service coordination and real-time updates, integrating safety-related information features, enabling customisation, providing motivational feedback and ensuring accessible customer support. While each mode presents distinct design considerations, they share overarching goals: enhancing usability, addressing mode-specific needs and priorities, reducing the environmental impact, providing meaningful motivations and incentives, and fostering sustained user engagement. The findings emphasise that the effectiveness of MaaS in facilitating sustainable behaviour is closely linked to the quality and availability of underlying transport services. Ultimately, this chapter highlights the need for holistic, constraint-informed interface design to ensure that MaaS platforms effectively reflect real-world conditions and offer realistic and comprehensive support for behaviour change and overall travel experience.

items.abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE - READ FIRST: This work is part of an open-book, AI-assisted research program. It was produced under bifurcated governance (a probabilistic AI agent drafts; a deterministic human key approves; a boundary-layer audit checks claims against receipt archives). Audit-and-correction is doctrine: superseded originals are preserved in version histories, corrections are disclosed amendments, and every significant test carries a preregistered falsifier in the append-only public ledger (github.com/LLong2026/four-horsemen). This paper is itself audited and contains a drift-audit case study of the AI-generated draft it replaced (Section 6). This software and its accompanying research are prototypes provided for educational and research purposes only; they are not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. Large language models are probabilistic systems whose outputs cannot, in general, be guaranteed correct. This paper documents deterministic caging: a probabilistic LLM placed inside a deterministic mathematical boundary that checks every state-changing output against preregistered, verifiable ground truth. The cage does not make the model right; it makes the model's errors detectable, bounded, and receipted. Contributions: (1) the bifurcated governance architecture with Substrate Determinism Receipts and preregistered falsifiers; (2) the field receipt of the first documented caging of a live LLM (Oct 8-9, 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23265723), where a pinned-model drift detection (confidence 0.92) produced a replayable cryptographic receipt that withstood direct third-party scrutiny; (3) a drift-audit case study in which the AI-generated draft of this very paper exhibited textbook confabulation - fabricated evaluation data, fabricated model attribution, and a fabricated institutional identity - and was caught by the same protocol the paper describes. The cage caught its own paper. Claims are deliberately scoped: one system, one event, full timestamped trail, publicly inspectable. items.title: DEVELOPING AUTONOMOUS CYBER DEFENCE SYSTEMS USING AI-DRIVEN INTRUSION DETECTION FOR IOT NETWORKS
items.abstract: As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues to grow exponentially, securing interconnected devices against evolving cyber threats has become paramount. This paper explores the development of an autonomous cyber defence system leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance intrusion detection for IoT networks. Traditional security measures fall short in resource-constrained, heterogeneous environments like IoT. Hence, we propose an AI-driven Intrusion Detection System (IDS) capable of real-time threat detection and autonomous response. Using a hybrid machine learning approach and reinforcement learning for automated mitigation, the system is evaluated on publicly available IoT security datasets. Results demonstrate improved detection accuracy, reduced false alarms, and efficient resource utilization. This research contributes to the advancement of intelligent, self-governing security mechanisms in IoT ecosystems.

items.title: Development of a small batch flexible station for packaging waste sorting in circular economy applications
items.abstract: Introduction Efficient packaging waste sorting is an important requirement for implementing circular economy strategies, yet many automated sorting solutions are designed for large-scale, high-throughput recycling facilities and are not well suited to small-batch industrial environments characterized by limited waste volumes, frequent material changes, and the need for rapid system reconfiguration. Methods This paper presents the design, implementation, and laboratory validation of a modular collaborative robotic workstation for small-batch packaging waste sorting. The proposed system integrates a collaborative robot, RGB-D vision system, conveyor-based material flow, and a ROS2-based control architecture within a unified perception–decision–manipulation framework. The perception pipeline combines class-agnostic segmentation using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with lightweight MobileNetV2-based classification for material recognition and is extended with optional modules for geometric reasoning and damage assessment. The proposed architecture reduces dependence on task-specific segmentation training and provides semantic information relevant to grasp planning, safety-aware task allocation, and human–robot collaboration. Results The workstation was validated under controlled laboratory conditions using three representative packaging waste categories: plastic bottles, aluminium cans, and Tetra Pak containers. The SAM + MobileNetV2 perception pipeline achieved an accuracy of 0.93, precision of 0.93, recall of 0.92, and F1-score of 0.92. System-level experiments demonstrated successful integration of RGB-D object localization, conveyor tracking, camera-to-robot coordinate transformation, and robotic pick-and-place execution. In contrast to conventional high-throughput sorting systems, the proposed workstation emphasizes modularity, flexibility, and collaborative operation for small-batch industrial packaging waste streams. In addition, workstation-level manipulation tests over 200 grasp attempts resulted in a 92.0% grasp success rate, an 89.0% end-to-end sorting success rate, and an estimated sorting rate of 5.73 picks/min under controlled conveyor-based conditions. Discussion The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating foundation-model-based perception with collaborative robot in a modular workstation intended for small-batch industrial packaging waste sorting. The proposed approach emphasizes flexibility, modularity, and reduced reconfiguration effort for variable waste streams. The results provide a basis for further development toward adaptive and human–robot collaborative sorting, while broader validation under more diverse, cluttered, and industrially representative conditions remains necessary.

items.title: Devising a Principled Rapid Guessing Workflow: Identification, Impact, and Treatment of Rapid Guessing in Cognitive Assessment
items.abstract: Abstract Low‐stakes assessments are particularly vulnerable to rapid guessing behavior, where responses may reflect minimal cognitive engagement, potentially biasing scores and weakening inferences. Drawing on a scoping review of more than 70 studies, we summarize how rapid guessing is identified, its impact on key parameters, and how it is treated. Detection methods range from time‐based thresholds to statistical models using response‐time or residual data, each balancing practicality and precision. Treatments include filtering, downweighting, and model‐based adjustments, with differing consequences for score meaning and comparability. However, decisions about identifying rapid guessing, evaluating its impact, and selecting treatments are often not explicitly linked, making it difficult to arrive at coherent analytic choices. To address this, we propose a four‐step workflow and reporting guidelines: (1) clarify construct relevance, (2) screen using context‐appropriate methods, (3) assess impact via sensitivity analysis, and (4) justify a treatment. Together, these tools provide a practical framework for defensible educational measurement practice.

items.title: Digital Human Modeling in Human–Robot Interaction
items.abstract: In human–robot collaboration, there are different levels of interaction. At lower levels, collisions must be avoided. At a higher level, collaborative robots directly interact with humans, and human health and safety need to be assured when designing work systems with robots included. In the process, adequate models of human motions are required. The diversity of human motions has led to ongoing research activities that have provided a considerable range of models. This chapter provides an overview of full-body human models such as kinematics, dynamics, and skin models and their applications in robotics. Kinematic models provide an abstraction of the human skeleton structure and its joints, whereas skin models provide mappings from the skeleton models to skin surfaces. Both are required for motion simulation with most human motion models. A survey of analytical, physics and data-driven human motion models is given. The state of the art as well as recent research advances are summarized for the models, and models of singular human motions and motion corridor/density models are differentiated. Their relevance for different levels of human–robot collaboration and ergonomics is discussed. Applications of motion models in the collaborative robotics domain and their respective advantages and shortcomings are reviewed with a special focus on their applicability for safety, efficiency and user experience in digital twins. Finally, the chapter presents three application scenarios in assembly lines and material handling in automotive industry.

items.title: Digital Impressions and Virtual Patient Applications in Prosthodontics
items.abstract: Digital impressions and virtual patient technologies have become integral components of prosthodontic workflows linking clinical data acquisition, diagnosis, treatment planning, and restoration fabrication. This chapter aims to evaluate the technical foundations, clinical applications, accuracy, and limitations of intraoral scanning and virtual patient technologies in the context of the current literature. The optical principles of intraoral scanners, three-dimensional data acquisition, and file formats such as STL, PLY, and OBJ are outlined. Accuracy, trueness, and precision are distinguished, and the effects of scanning extent, scanning strategy, operator experience, preparation geometry, moisture control, and implant scan body characteristics on impression outcomes are considered. Indication-dependent applications of digital impressions in tooth-supported fixed restorations, implant-supported prostheses, and removable prosthodontics are compared with conventional techniques. Virtual patient construction is examined through the integration of intraoral scans, three-dimensional facial scans, cone-beam computed tomography, digital photographs, and mandibular motion records. Data registration, virtual articulators, digital facebows, and the transition from static three-dimensional models to dynamic four-dimensional representations are discussed. Although digital workflows may facilitate data exchange, visualization, and patient communication, full-arch and completely edentulous cases remain challenging because of recording accuracy, soft-tissue dynamics, interoperability, and costs. The potential of artificial intelligence-assisted design and individualized planning is considered alongside limitations in the available clinical evidence. Overall, digital impressions and virtual patient technologies should not be regarded as universal replacements for conventional procedures. Instead, they represent complementary tools whose use should be guided by clinical indication, required accuracy, patient-specific conditions, and available resources. The chapter emphasizes that technical feasibility alone does not establish clinical superiority and that careful validation is needed before emerging dynamic and artificial intelligence-based approaches are routinely implemented.

items.title: Digital Readiness for Technology-Enhanced Undergraduate Research
items.abstract: As undergraduate research increasingly relies on digital databases, analytical software, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled technologies, research learning is potentially mediated through digital infrastructures that enable students to engage in knowledge construction. However, disparities in technological access and institutional support may constrain these learning opportunities. Guided by van Dijk’s digital divide model and Ragnedda’s concept of digital capital, this study employed interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) to examine how undergraduate students experienced digital readiness during the research process. Data were generated through three rounds of in-depth interviews with each of the eight undergraduate researchers at a Vietnamese public university. Analysis revealed that limited access to scholarly databases and research software usually restricted students’ engagement with technology-enhanced research learning. In addition, the absence of clear institutional policies and guidance regarding AI technologies potentially generated uncertainty about acceptable AI practices and contributed to uneven development of students’ digital competencies. These technological constraints influenced many students’ academic self-efficacy and reduced their ability to transform digital resources into meaningful learning and research outcomes. The effectiveness of technology-supported undergraduate research might depend not only on the availability of digital tools but also on equitable access, AI literacy development, and institutional support structures. The study contributes to the field of technologies in learning by demonstrating how digital infrastructure and technology governance may shape students’ participation in research-based learning. Implications are offered for the design of inclusive technology-enabled learning environments that support equitable undergraduate research engagement.

items.title: DIGITAL STORYTELLING AND NARRATIVE IN THE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AGE: TRANSFORMING CREATIVITY, COMMUNICATION, AND HUMAN EXPERIENCE
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the landscape of digital storytelling, reshaping how narratives are created, shared, and experienced across various digital platforms. From automated content generation and interactive storytelling to virtual reality experiences and personalized narratives, AI has become an influential creative partner in media production, education, entertainment, journalism, marketing, and cultural preservation. This paper examines the evolving relationship between digital storytelling and artificial intelligence, focusing on how AI influences creativity, communication, and human experience. Using a qualitative review of existing literature, the study explores the historical evolution of storytelling, the emergence of AI-powered narrative systems, and the opportunities and challenges associated with AI-assisted creativity. The paper also discusses ethical concerns, including algorithmic bias, misinformation, copyright ownership, authenticity, and the changing role of human creators. Findings suggest that while AI enhances efficiency, personalization, and audience engagement, human imagination, emotional intelligence, cultural awareness, and ethical judgment remain indispensable components of meaningful storytelling. The study concludes that the future of storytelling lies in collaborative intelligence, where humans and AI work together to produce innovative, inclusive, and emotionally resonant narratives.

items.title: Digital Transformation and Multidsciplinary Treatment Approaches in Orthodontics
items.abstract: Digital transformation in orthodontics refers to the digitization of patients’ clinical, photographic, radiological, and surface data; the integration of these data within a common digital environment; and the management of the workflow from diagnosis to retention based on these data. Intraoral scanners, digital models, cone-beam computed tomography, three-dimensional cephalometry, virtual treatment setups, clear aligner systems, artificial intelligence, and remote monitoring platforms contribute to making orthodontic decisions more measurable, reproducible, and shareable. Nevertheless, it should be recognized that digital tools do not inherently guarantee clinical success and that data quality, biological boundaries, operator supervision, and the sequencing of multidisciplinary treatment are decisive determinants of outcomes. This chapter addresses digital diagnostic and record-taking methods in orthodontics, intraoral scanning, three-dimensional and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric assessment, digital treatment planning, clear aligner workflows, and teleorthodontics. In addition, decision-making and treatment sequencing are discussed in multidisciplinary clinical situations involving impacted teeth, endodontically treated teeth, patients with periodontal problems, missing teeth, and orthodontic preparation before prosthetic treatment. The monitoring of biological risks, particularly root resorption, using digital data; the limitations of digital orthodontics; and the future transition toward personalized treatment models are also evaluated. The fundamental approach is to use digital technology not as a substitute for clinical examination, but as a decision-support system that addresses the appropriate clinical question and strengthens communication among specialists.

items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, understanding whether students possess the foundational conditions needed to benefit from AI-mediated learning has become an important educational challenge. This study conceptualizes dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning as the configuration of ICT self-efficacy, attitudes toward technology and expectations of future ICT use that may support meaningful engagement with AI-mediated learning environments, and examines how these configurations relate to objectively assessed digital competence and to student characteristics. ICILS 2023 contains no measure of AI literacy or AI use, so these are candidate foundations rather than a direct measure of preparedness for AI. Using data from 118,764 Grade-8 students across 35 education systems participating in the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS 2023), we conducted sampling-weighted latent profile analyses on four internationally comparable indicators. Computer and information literacy (CIL) was examined as an external criterion using the BCH approach, and profile membership was predicted by socioeconomic background, gender, educational aspirations and ICT access. Four profiles emerged: average (55.9%), attitude-oriented (25.2%), low-disposition (11.0%) and efficacy-dominant (7.9%). Differences in CIL across profiles were modest, and students in the efficacy-dominant profile, who reported ICT self-efficacy more than two standard deviations above the mean, did not outperform the average profile in objectively assessed competence, a pattern we interpret as a confidence-competence mismatch rather than as high preparedness. On a common metric of average marginal effects, gender showed larger and more consistent contrasts than socioeconomic background. These findings suggest that the dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning are distinct from computer and information literacy and should be understood as a multidimensional configuration of learner characteristics whose relevance to actual AI-mediated learning remains to be tested directly.

items.title: Distilling First-Principles Accuracy into Compact Machine Learning Potentials for Condensed-Phase Chemistry
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have made first-principles-quality potential energy surfaces increasingly accessible for condensed-phase chemistry, but their inference cost can still limit the sampling needed to compute experimentally relevant observables. In this work, we use knowledge distillation to construct compact “student” models that retain the accuracy of much larger “teacher” models obtained through either finetuning of foundation models or Δ-learning. The resulting students reduce production simulation cost by approximately an order of magnitude, making high-accuracy sampling practical for challenging condensed-phase problems. We demonstrate this across three problems of increasing sampling complexity: finite-temperature NPT simulations of ice Ih, classical and path-integral simulations of liquid water over 240–370 K, and path-integral umbrella-sampling simulations of water dissociation at the anatase TiO2(101)/water interface. When compared, the distilled students reproduce the target observables of their teachers more reliably than equally compact models trained only on the available reference data. The liquid water student, distilled from a Δ-learned CCSD(T)-quality teacher, reproduces thermodynamic, structural, transport, and nuclear quantum effects over the full temperature range studied. At the TiO2/water interface, knowledge distillation makes PIMD umbrella sampling practical and shows that nuclear quantum effects lower the dissociation barrier by approximately 2 kcal/mol and shift the molecular–dissociated free energy difference into closer agreement with recent solid-state 17O NMR measurements. Our work demonstrates how knowledge distillation can make accurate MLIPs practical for the sampling methods needed to connect condensed-phase reaction thermodynamics with experiment, notably for interfacial chemistry and catalysis.

items.title: Do People Dream of Sex with Androids? Neuroscience Behind Cybersex and Technosexual Behaviour
items.abstract: Technology-mediated sexual behaviours, including cybersex and technosex, are becoming increasingly prevalent as digital technologies, virtual reality, artificial intelligence, and interactive devices continue to develop. Although these behaviours may offer numerous benefits, such as facilitating sexual exploration, supporting individuals with disabilities, and enabling long-distance intimacy, they may also contribute to problematic patterns of use in some individuals. This review synthesises current knowledge on the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms underlying cybersex and technosexual behaviour. The article discusses conceptual and definitional issues, epidemiological data, and theoretical frameworks, including the Triple A model and the “quasi-necrophilia” framework, to explain the characteristics and motivations behind technology-mediated sexual activities. Furthermore, it summarises psychological factors associated with both adaptive and maladaptive use, emphasising the role of emotion regulation, personality traits, neurodevelopmental conditions, mental health, and sexual motivations. The review also presents current evidence on the neurobiology of cybersex and technosex, highlighting the involvement of dopaminergic reward pathways and similarities to other reward-related behaviours. Finally, available approaches to the treatment of problematic technology-mediated sexual behaviour are discussed, including pharmacotherapy, as well as psychoeducation and psychotherapy, with particular attention to the importance of addressing underlying psychological conditions. The article argues that cybersex and technosex should not be inherently pathologised—instead, they should be understood within a biopsychosocial framework that distinguishes between healthy sexual expression and clinically significant impairment.

items.title: Do-It-with-AI Framework for Invention: A Kundt’s Tube Case Study
items.abstract: This exploratory case study examines the feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) into a low-cost Kundt’s tube activity in pre-service science teacher education. The proposed Do-It-With-AI framework comprises four phases: conceptual exploration, design development, troubleshooting, and extension to real-world applications. Scopus AI was used to support the literature-oriented conceptual exploration, while ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-5 supported the generation of design alternatives, troubleshooting hypotheses, and possible extensions. Three pre-service teachers constructed and tested the apparatus, and successive configurations were evaluated through resonance measurements and estimation of the speed of sound. The case illustrates how AI-generated suggestions can be incorporated into an iterative design–test–verification process in which proposed modifications are examined against physical principles and experimental evidence. The four-phase sequence is therefore presented as a feasible framework for integrating generative AI with hands-on experimentation, with instructor-guided verification serving as an essential component. Because the present study focuses on feasibility and process rather than educational outcomes, further investigation with larger cohorts and explicit measures of student reasoning, learning, collaboration, and AI literacy is required. The principal contribution of the Kundt’s tube case is to demonstrate a structured and empirically grounded use of generative AI in low-cost experimental development within pre-service science teacher education.

items.title: Domain-Sensitive Patterns in Student Writing: Comparing Human, AI-Revised, and AI-Generated Abstracts in Human Factors
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in academic writing, although many studies compare only human-written and AI-generated text. This within-subjects study examined manual, AI-revised, and AI-generated extended abstracts in a graduate human factors course. Text analyses included 96 abstracts from 32 participants, and repeated-measures survey analyses included 30 participants. We compared structural and lexical features, readability, Sentence-BERT embeddings, exploratory writing-condition classification, technology acceptance, and perceived workload. Manual abstracts showed the greatest variability. AI-generated abstracts showed less structural variability, higher lexical density, and greater estimated reading difficulty. AI-revised abstracts showed metric-specific overlap with both other conditions. A three-class classifier yielded 68.75% accuracy under abstract-level leave-one-out cross-validation, although participant and topic overlap limits generalization. Participants reported greater acceptance and lower workload in the AI-supported conditions. These preliminary findings motivate examining degrees of AI involvement and using participant-grouped validation in future studies.

items.title: Ecological Invisibility in Classroom AI Use: Rethinking Pedagogical Efficiency, Sustainability and Teacher Agency
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in everyday teaching, yet its environmental costs remain largely absent from how educators reason about its use. This study examines how 22 teachers working in public schools in Türkiye, each with at least one academic year of experience integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom, interpret and navigate these technologies at the intersection of pedagogical effectiveness, professional responsibility, and ecological sustainability. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed through Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis within a generic interpretive qualitative design. Five themes were developed. The first three show teachers actively mediating AI through pedagogical judgment, a restructured professional agency, and a renewed relational and epistemic role. The study’s central contribution lies in the final two: for almost all participants, AI’s ecological cost was not unknown but rendered invisible in everyday practice—a professionally produced ordering of attention enacted through the very pedagogical agency that makes teachers effective. When this cost surfaced, teachers managed rather than resolved the tension through pedagogical rationalization and self-reported intentions toward ecologically motivated restraint, while extending their moral concern to students’ cognitive dependence. Ecological invisibility thus emerges not as a knowledge deficit but as a by-product of professional attention—one that teacher education and policy should address through a critical AI literacy integrating ethical, ecological, and pedagogical dimensions.

items.title: Education and Nation-Building: Revisiting Mahamana Madan Mohan Malaviya's Vision in the Light of the National Education Policy 2020
items.abstract: Education has a long association with nation building, social change, and human development. Mahamana Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya believed that education is necessary for the development of character, national consciousness, social responsibility and a self-reliant nation. The objective of his education was to bring together Indian cultural traditions with moral values and Indian spiritual ideals with modern science, technical knowledge, vocational competence and research. The institutionalisation of this vision was in the form of Banaras Hindu University, which aimed at integrating Indian knowledge traditions with modern education and professional training. This present study focuses on Malaviya's Educational Philosophy and its relevance in the present context in the National Education Policy 2020. The study is qualitative in nature and descriptive and analytical in design and relied entirely on secondary sources like the speeches and writings of Malaviya, institutional documents of BHU, National Education Policy 2020, Indian knowledge system guidelines and relevant academic literature. This analysis is based on five dimensions namely holistic and value-based education, education for nation-building, empowerment of teacher, skill and vocational education and integration of Indian Knowledge Systems with modern scientific knowledge. The study finds significant conceptual relevance of Malaviya’s educational ideas with NEP 2020. Both approaches view education as a way of building intellectually capable, ethically responsible, socially sensitive, culturally rooted and professionally competent citizens. Yet, Malaviya’s ideas should not be mechanically adopted. Its modern relevance requires a critical engagement with constitutional values, pluralism, scientific temper, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, social diversity and changing employment requirements. The paper concludes that Malaviya’s educational vision can provide an important philosophical basis for implementing NEP 2020 and developing an inclusive, innovative, self-reliant and socially responsible India.

items.title: Effects of Monitoring and Outcome Pressure on Skilled Typists’ Performance
items.abstract: Choking under pressure refers to suboptimal performance under stressful conditions in an individual who, based on prior performance, would be expected to perform at a higher level. Although most observed in sports, choking can occur in musical performance, test-taking, and other skilled domains. The present study used typing to examine the effects of monitoring pressure, outcome pressure, and task difficulty on the cognitive processes underlying typing. Seventy-six undergraduates were randomly assigned to one of four between-subjects conditions: control, monitoring pressure (video camera), outcome pressure (monetary competition), or combined pressure. Participants copy-typed high- and low-frequency four-letter words; reaction time to first keystroke (RT1), inter-keystroke interval (IKSI), and error rate indexed outer-loop, inner-loop, and accuracy processes respectively. Results revealed no evidence of choking under any pressure condition, but consistent task difficulty effects: low-frequency words slowed both RT1 and IKSI. These findings suggest typing is resilient to moderate pressure and highlight its promise as an accessible testbed for choking research.

items.title: Efficacy of artificial intelligence-driven conversational agents (chatbots) for mental health promotion among university students: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background University students experience substantial mental-health burdens, while access to timely support remains uneven. AI conversational agents may provide low-threshold support, but the evidence base has expanded rapidly and prior reviews have often combined different age groups, intervention types, outcome domains, and comparator conditions. Objective To evaluate the effects of AI-mediated conversational interventions on depressive and anxiety symptoms in university students, while distinguishing outcome domains, comparator intensity, intervention architecture, and the evidential requirements for standardized post-intervention effect estimation. Methods We updated the search in PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and Web of Science to the revised search date and rebuilt an auditable cross-database record ledger. The updated workflow included 3,786 exported records, 451 DOI/PMID duplicates, 41 confirmed title/author duplicates, and 3,294 unique records screened. All title/abstract records completed a two-reviewer screening and consensus chain. Forty-six update-search records entered research-level/full-text assessment. Randomized controlled trials were eligible for causal quantitative synthesis; relevant feasibility, acceptability, usability, and non-comparable controlled studies were retained narratively. Standard post-intervention analyses used Hedges g, REML random-effects models, and Hartung-Knapp adjustment, and were restricted to attributable two-group post-intervention data. Results In the final locked non-active/low-intensity comparator analysis, three depression comparisons favored conversational interventions (k=3; Hedges g=-0.413, 95% CI -0.557 to -0.268; I2 = 0.0%) and four anxiety comparisons also favored them (k=4; Hedges g=-0.435, 95% CI -0.603 to -0.268; I2 = 2.1%). In the separate active conversational-control analysis, two MYLO comparisons did not show a reliable incremental effect for depression (k=2; g=0.165, 95% CI -0.580 to 0.911) or anxiety (k=2; g=0.190, 95% CI -0.556 to 0.937). The evidence base remained small, clinically heterogeneous, and limited by attrition, self-reported outcomes, and uncertainty regarding generalizability. Conclusions AI conversational interventions may improve depressive and anxiety symptoms relative to non-active or low-intensity comparators in university students, but the certainty of evidence is low and estimates are based on few comparisons. Evidence against active conversational controls is very uncertain. Outcome-domain differences and architecture-related claims should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Secure, consent-based, human-supervised implementation and objective outcome assessment are priorities for future research. items.abstract: Metaverse, a virtual shared space, is a promising avenue for transforming supply chain operations through emerging trends and technologies shaping the future of suppliers, manufacturers, retailers, and customers. This chapter examines the emerging trends and technologies that are shaping the future of the supply chain metaverse. Emerging trends include advanced virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and digital twins, which are creating immersive and interactive spaces for stakeholders to interact with digital representations of supply chain operations. Artificial intelligence and machine learning provide data-driven optimization, and the metaverse can be used to simulate different scenarios, test new solutions, and optimize processes based on real-time data analysis. Additionally, blockchain ensures secure, transparent record-keeping for product provenance, reducing fraud and improving compliance. Furthermore, this chapter provides practical scenarios on how the supply chain metaverse can improve transparency and increase agility. Finally, this chapter concludes by acknowledging the need for interdisciplinary research and collaboration to address the challenges and unlock the full potential of the supply chain metaverse.

items.title: Emotion-Centric Customer Segmentation and Loyalty Strategies in the Era of Generative AI
items.abstract: In many segmentation approaches, customer identity and purchase behaviour are emphasised, while the emotional experience of the customer–brand relationship is often overlooked. This conceptual paper proposes the Emotion-Centric Customer Segmentation and Loyalty (ECSL) framework for the generative AI era, linking emotional foundations (emotions, attachment, and perceived experience quality) to emotion-centric segmentation and AI-enabled interaction fit (tone, offers, service scripts, and journey orchestration). AI and generative AI are positioned as enablers that help sense emotional cues and support segment-fit responses across touchpoints. Value co-creation behaviours and loyalty outcomes (retention, commitment, advocacy) are presented as downstream results, while ethical governance and trust (transparency, consent, fairness, accountability, and human oversight) are treated as essential conditions that strengthen or weaken these effects. Directions are outlined for future empirical testing of the model and its moderation mechanisms.

items.title: Emotional Comfort at a Cost: The Dynamic Role of Social Chatbot Use in Daily Loneliness, Well-Being, and Interpersonal Interaction
items.abstract: As generative AI chatbots increasingly serve as emotional companions, understanding their implications for users’ emotional and social lives is critical. This 14-day diary study involving 97 social chatbot users examined how daily loneliness relates to chatbot engagement and subsequent psychosocial outcomes. Bayesian multilevel models showed that on days when participants felt lonelier than usual, they reported longer chatbot use and stronger emotional engagement. Notably, these two forms of engagement showed distinct associations with daily outcomes. Emotional engagement was associated with higher daily subjective well-being but shorter interpersonal interaction duration, whereas longer usage duration was associated with lower interpersonal interaction pleasure. Mediation analyses reflected the same patterns. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing behavioral from emotional engagement with social chatbots and suggest that emotional benefits and interpersonal costs may coexist in everyday human–AI interaction, informing the responsible design and balanced use of social AI companions.

items.title: Emotional design and advertising: a systematic review of the literature on consumer behavior
items.abstract: Introduction Emotional design integrates sensory, functional, social, and symbolic elements to elicit affective responses that may influence consumer perception, attitudes, and behavior. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between emotional design, advertising, and consumer behavior based on recent scientific literature. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines. Searches were performed in Scopus and Web of Science, and 66 primary studies published during the last ten years were included. Results The reviewed evidence shows that emotional design strategies incorporate perceptual stimuli, user experiences, and meaning-making processes. Color, shape, texture, packaging, and multisensory stimuli contribute to attraction, attention, and perceived quality, while usability, ergonomics, interactivity, and demonstrations enhance the user experience. Storytelling, cultural identity, sustainability, and personalization contribute to meaning construction and strengthen consumer-brand connections. The literature also identifies positive, negative, and complex emotions, including pleasure, trust, fear, guilt, nostalgia, attachment, and identification, which are associated with purchase intention, satisfaction, loyalty, repurchase, and other consumer responses. Discussion The findings indicate that emotional design operates across sensory, experiential, social, and symbolic dimensions, extending its influence beyond immediate purchase decisions toward longer-term consumer-brand relationships. However, the methodological diversity of the reviewed studies highlights the need for more integrated approaches combining subjective, physiological, and digital measures to evaluate emotional and behavioral responses. items.title: Employee AI readiness and the leadership gap: a theory-informed commentary on a CIO.com feature
items.abstract: This paper offers a theory-informed commentary on the executive-employee gap in enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) readiness, using a CIO.com feature on employee AI optimism and an AI leadership gap as its focal practitioner text. Rather than treating the article as empirical evidence, the paper interprets it through scholarship on socio-technical change, organizational readiness, AI governance, work design, and incentive alignment, using 2024-2025 industry reports as context. It examines how the text frames the readiness gap, how socio-technical and incentive-alignment perspectives explain it, and what operational risks may follow. The analysis suggests the leadership gap is better understood as an organizational-design problem than as employee resistance or a training deficit. When AI tools are introduced without changes to workflows, governance, learning, and accountability, employees may face burdens and uncertainty about legitimate AI use. The paper contributes by framing AI readiness as an organizational condition, integrating socio-technical and incentive-alignment perspectives, identifying shadow AI, weak output validation, data-quality problems, and accountability ambiguity as risk pathways, and proposing a Socio-Technical AI Readiness Framework linking AI pressure, readiness architecture, employee readiness, operational transformation, and risk leakage. For managers, sustainable AI transformation requires credible organizational conditions for AI-enabled work, not merely greater tool use.

items.title: Empowering the supply chain workforce
items.abstract: The metaverse has emerged as a transformative virtual environment where individuals interact digitally, offering significant potential for supply chain operations through real-time tracking capabilities. This technological evolution has enhanced business efficiency by reducing costs and improving transparency across multiple operational levels. By combining augmented reality, virtual reality, and artificial intelligence, the metaverse creates immersive, interactive spaces for work, training, and collaboration. This chapter examines how metaverse technologies are revolutionizing human resource functions—particularly workforce training and skill development within supply chain management. It investigates how the metaverse establishes innovative learning environments that transform workforce development in logistics, warehouse management, and related fields. Using a qualitative research methodology, this work comprehensively reviews the existing literature to understand connections between metaverse applications and supply chain workforce skill enhancement. The research includes case analyses of organizations that have implemented metaverse-based training in their supply chain operations. This chapter incorporates perspectives from industry professionals regarding metaverse training adoption processes, implementation challenges, and effectiveness metrics. Research findings strongly indicate that metaverse-driven training and skill development initiatives have substantially improved workforce efficiency and enhanced employee knowledge retention. However, this chapter also addresses significant challenges, including high infrastructure costs, shortages of qualified trainers, and ethical considerations.

items.title: Enabling Innovation through Workplace Spirituality: Insights from Indonesian Information Professionals
items.abstract: Background Public-sector information institutions operate amid continuous change, rising service demands, and complex tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources and Conservation of Resources perspectives, this study examines whether workplace spirituality functions as a motivational resource linking job characteristics, transformational leadership, and coworker incivility to innovative work behavior (IWB) among information professionals. Method A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 150 employees of Indonesian public libraries (n = 93) and archives (n = 57). Hypotheses were tested with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), including assessment of discriminant validity (Fornell–Larcker, HTMT), collinearity (VIF), effect sizes (f 2 ), predictive relevance (Q 2 ), and model fit (SRMR). Result Workplace spirituality showed the strongest association with IWB (β = 0.652) and accounted for a substantial share of the associations of job characteristics (indirect β = 0.437) and transformational leadership (indirect β = 0.093) with IWB, indicating complementary partial mediation rather than full mediation. The total effect of coworker incivility on IWB was not significant (β = 0.105); its association operated indirectly through workplace spirituality (β = −0.078). The model explained 63.0% of the variance in workplace spirituality and 68.5% in IWB, with predictive relevance established (Q 2 = 0.325 and 0.434). These patterns are consistent with a model in which structural and interpersonal work conditions relate to innovation largely — though not exclusively — through employees’ experienced meaning, community, and value congruence, although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Conclusion The findings suggest that cultivating workplace spirituality (meaningful work, sense of community, value alignment), enriching job design, and curbing coworker incivility may support innovation in public libraries and archives. Generalization to galleries and museums awaits further research.

items.title: Engaging With Wicked Problems: Patterns of Success and Failure
items.abstract: Some of the toughest problems corporations, organizations, and societies face are wicked problems. Conventional or “tame” problems have right answers and best choices that can be determined using analytical methods. In contrast, wicked problems ( Rittel & Webber, 1973 ) are impossible to solve definitively but can only be managed because they are big, messy, laden with unintended consequences, and filled with conflict between stakeholders who have multiple competing interests. Analytical methods designed for conventional problems won’t work effectively against problems like illegal drugs, societal inequality, poverty, debt, war, or homelessness. We conducted an investigation of 32 actual wicked or near-wicked problems to identify practices that seemed effective and those that failed to work or even got in the way of progress. We found that progress depended on revising goals, aligning the goals of multiple stakeholders, and reframing the way the situation is understood. From this investigation, we formulated a set of recommendations. These include judging whether a problem is wicked, and if so shifting mindset to a flexible perspective, and making use of relevant tools, along with mistakes to avoid. We also suggest a potentially positive perspective on wicked problems—that in some situations they can support change and adaptation rather than rigidity and conformity.

items.title: Entrepreneurship and creative destruction: the enduring relevance of Schumpeter in the age of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to reexamine Schumpeter’s framework of entrepreneurship and creative destruction to assess its explanatory power in artificial intelligence (AI)-intensive capitalism, where algorithmic technologies reshape the structural conditions under which entrepreneurial agency and innovation unfold. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a conceptual reinterpretation approach grounded in a close reading of Schumpeter’s principal texts, placing this reconstruction in dialogue with contemporary literature on AI and entrepreneurship, as well as with post-Schumpeterian patterns, including Schumpeter Mark I, Mark II and intellectual monopoly dynamics. Findings Moreover, AI confirmed the Schumpeterian conceptual core, radicalised its dynamics through temporal compression and ecosystemic displacement and necessitated a partial reformulation. Entrepreneurial judgement under radical uncertainty remained irreducible, although agency became distributed across hybrid human-algorithmic configurations where formative creativity grows increasingly automatable, while transformative creativity was dependent on human judgement. Creative destruction shifts towards platform-governed ecosystemic architectures and the prevailing Schumpeterian pattern depends on each sector’s appropriability and governance conditions, rather than on the technology itself. Where intellectual monopoly dynamics prevail, innovation is co-produced across the periphery and the capture of its returns concentrates asymmetrically at the nucleus. Originality/value This study rethinks the relationship between entrepreneurship, creative destruction and AI by reinterpreting the internal tensions in Schumpeter’s work. Based on this reconstruction, it develops a framework of distributed agency and ecosystemic creative destruction centred on the distinction between formative and transformative creativity at the institutional level and identifies the appropriate conditions under which innovation generates structural discontinuities. This further shows that the Schumpeterian patterns associated with AI emerge from sector-specific configurations of appropriability and governance, providing a structural explanation that previous management literature had left underdeveloped.

items.title: Ergonomics, Values and Robot Ethics
items.abstract: The development, implementation and use of technological artifacts introduces ethical issues—technologies are not ethically neutral. This ethical dimension is particularly obvious in robotic technologies, as many types and applications of robots are situated at the intersection of automation and social interaction. Consequently, developers, researchers and users of robots are confronted with ethical issues, for example concerning safety or (human) autonomy. With respect to ergonomics, two main themes can be identified: (1) Ergonomics itself involves certain values such as well-being, accessibility, performance optimization, safety, and trust. These values (and others) can and should be discussed in ethical terms. (2) Complex ethical issues in human–robot interaction are often difficult to address and can be cognitively overwhelming in the design process. items.title: Ethical Appraisals of Artificial Intelligence in MBA Education: Moral Concern, Social Pressure, Perceived Benefits, and AI Experience
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined how MBA students appraise ethical concerns, practical benefits, social expectations, control, and institutional governance related to educational artificial intelligence (AI). The analysis used 275 eligible responses submitted by the prespecified study cut-off. Descriptive statistics, omega and Spearman-Brown reliability, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), rank-based and bootstrap robustness checks, and regression models of ordered AI experience were used. Three exploratory dimensions were retained in 90.4% of 500 bootstrap samples. A proportional-odds reference model improved on the null model, chi-square(6) = 17.81, p = .007, but the proportional-odds assumption was rejected, chi-square(6) = 17.81, p = .007; threshold-specific models were therefore primary. AI self-efficacy/control was associated with reporting at least moderate rather than none/minimal AI experience (OR = 1.51, 95% CI [1.13, 2.03], p = .005), and this result persisted after background adjustment, bootstrap validation, and response-quality screens. In the smaller extensive-experience comparison (n = 26), efficiency benefit and perceived ethical-issue frequency were positive exploratory correlates. Concern was highest for data privacy, while governance responses indicated comparatively limited knowledge of personal-data practices. Predictive performance was modest. The findings support clearer task-specific guidance, critical AI literacy, and transparent data practices, but the cross-sectional self-report design does not establish causal adoption effects or validated moral profiles

items.title: Ethical Generative AI Use in Higher Education: An Action Research Study Using the Think Aloud Method
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, it presents significant challenges related to ethical use, academic integrity and students' potential over‐reliance on AI‐generated outputs. The Think Aloud method offers a pedagogical approach for making students' reasoning visible as they interact with generative AI tools. Objective This mixed‐methods action research study explored the role of the Think Aloud method as a pedagogical intervention in supporting students' metacognitive awareness and ethical engagement with generative AI tools in a first‐year entrepreneurship course. Method Data were collected through reflective journals, classroom observations and a post‐intervention survey. The study involved 44 first‐year undergraduate students, with 38 students completing the post‐intervention survey. Qualitative data were analysed thematically, while survey responses were examined using descriptive statistics and an exploratory correlation analysis. Results and Conclusions Findings suggested that Think Aloud supported students' emerging awareness of prompt construction, verification practices and ethical decision‐making when using generative AI. However, students' critical evaluation of AI‐generated content often remained at a surface level, particularly among students requiring additional support. The study indicates that Think Aloud can make students' AI‐related reasoning more visible and can support more intentional engagement with generative AI, but it should not be viewed as a stand‐alone solution. Rather, it appears most effective when embedded within a broader pedagogical framework that includes AI literacy, prompt engineering, verification strategies and evaluative judgement. The study contributes classroom‐based evidence on process‐oriented approaches to ethical generative AI use in higher education and highlights the need for sustained instructional scaffolding to support deeper critical engagement with AI tools.

items.title: Ethical Hyper-Personalised Emotional Branding
items.abstract: This abstract discuss how neuromarketing and generative AI converge to allow hyper-personalized emotional branding. It suggests the Ethical Adaptive Emotional Narrative Framework, a theoretical concept that brings in emotional data analysis, AI-generated marketing content, and is in line with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The framework categorizes emotionally adaptive marketing into four processes that are data capture, emotion inference, generative content adaptation and feedback learning. Every stage includes protection mechanisms, like approval, transparency, proportionality, and human control, to avoid manipulation and ensure the freedom of consumers. The chapter, by introducing the principle of emotional integrity, shows how organizations can use emotionally responsive AI systems to engage and build trust and yet remain ethically accountable and compliant with regulations.

items.title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Emergency Triage Using Synthetic Clinical Dialogues: Toward a Multimodal Clinical Safety Framework
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Prioritizing patient safety through accurate emergency triage is critical during mass-gathering events such as Hajj and Umrah, where high patient volumes can significantly increase the risk of clinical errors. Although the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) provides a standardized triage protocol, it remains dependent on human judgment, while traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models often struggle to capture the nuanced clinical context embedded in patient narratives. To address this gap, this study evaluates GPT-5.2 using synthetically generated dialogues as a step toward a conceptual clinical decision-support framework that bridges structured electronic health records (EHRs) with triage interactions through clinical dialogues. By combining narrative inputs with structured physiological indicators, it explores the potential to support more informed clinical decision-making under controlled simulation conditions. Methods: To evaluate this contribution, we systematically assessed the role of clinical dialogues in triage performance using a balanced and stratified dataset of 1000 simulated Hajj-context scenarios. Results: The results demonstrate that incorporating clinical dialogues can significantly improve triage performance, with a 79.7% relative reduction in under-triage across all ESI levels. A more noticeable improvement was observed in high-acuity cases, with a 91.9% relative reduction in under-triage. In addition, the model achieved a high-acuity recall of 94.5%, highlighting its ability to identify critical “red-flag” symptoms that are often not captured in structured data. These findings suggest that narrative context may contribute to more accurate triage assessment and improved identification of high-acuity cases. Conclusions: Consequently, when evaluated within a controlled decision-support setting, this study suggests that large language model (LLM)-based systems may improve triage reliability and may contribute to safer triage decision-making in high-demand clinical environments.

items.title: Evaluation of large language models for ICI-related liver injury with an emerging microbiome focus
items.abstract: Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related liver injury (ICI-LI) has heterogeneous phenotypes, a complex differential diagnosis, and evolving management. Gut microbiome research provides biological plausibility for immune regulation during ICI therapy, but evidence specific to ICI-LI remains limited and is not yet clinically actionable. We evaluated whether publicly accessible large language model (LLM) chatbots can organize this mixed evidence base and communicate its uncertainty. Methods We developed a disease-specific benchmark of 25 questions covering immunological mechanisms, microbiome and immune regulation, diagnosis, biomarkers, and management of ICI-LI. The benchmark addressed ICI-LI broadly and included a focused microbiome component. Four publicly available LLM platforms were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, the Global Quality Score, the JAMA Benchmark Criteria, and six readability indices. These instruments assessed information quality, structure, transparency, and patient-facing readability rather than factual accuracy or clinical decision-making. Results Performance differed across DISCERN, EQIP, and JAMA scores, whereas the Global Quality Score showed limited discrimination. Question-level variation was most apparent for items requiring evidence appraisal or translation. All platforms produced structured responses, but none met the prespecified patient-facing readability benchmark. Readability was interpreted separately from clinician-facing information synthesis. Conclusions Disease-specific multidimensional evaluation is needed before LLM-generated information can be considered reliable for microbiome-informed clinical communication or decision support. Evaluation should emphasize evidence calibration and distinguish biological plausibility, association, and clinically actionable evidence.

items.title: Evidence Is the Key, Not the Log: Cryptographic Execution Control for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems
items.abstract: What if an AI agent could not complete a consequential action until the real-world result of an earlier, bounded action had been independently verified—and that verification was required to unlock the next execution step? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly operate financial systems, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, autonomous machinery, and critical infrastructure, conventional security mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: authorization establishes what is permitted, but does not necessarily establish what actually happened along the real execution path. Audit logs may record a mistake after its consequences become irreversible. Simulations may succeed while the real destination, network route, transaction system, or physical actuator behaves differently. Even a successful initial authorization does not justify unlimited authority to execute subsequent actions. This paper develops a different architectural principle: “Evidence is the key, not the log.” Building on the distinction that computation is not authority to act, the proposed architecture makes independently validated evidence of a preceding real effect a technical prerequisite for later effectuation. The mechanism is called Receipt-Gated Staged Effectuation, supported by an Interim Effectuation Validator (IEV). For selected consequential operations, the architecture authorizes a deliberately bounded but real first effect, rather than immediately releasing the complete consequence. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network element, storage component, or hardware controller generates an Effect Confirmation Receipt (ECR) describing what actually occurred. The IEV independently verifies the receipt against the authorized Candidate Act, expected effect, phase, destination, sink identity, freshness, policy, revocation state, and authorized scope. Only after successful validation does the protected domain establish the Continuation Authority Object (CAO) required for the next phase. The critical distinction is that the next effect can be made technically impossible—not merely prohibited by policy—until validated evidence from the preceding real effect becomes available. Possible implementations include receipt-derived cryptographic keys, split-key reconstruction, protected internal state, hardware latches, pre-staged non-executable commands, and pre-delivered ciphertext whose final decryption material remains withheld. Unlike ordinary canary deployment or post-execution monitoring, the earlier phase's evidence becomes part of the causal authority chain. Its receipt is not merely information about the previous operation; it is a required input to the authority enabling the next operation. The paper develops: Three effectuation modes: Direct protected single-phase execution, bounded demonstration followed by full effectuation, and progressive multi-phase execution. Adaptive effectuation: Geometric and risk-dependent progression, reversibility-aware phase sizing, nested stages, and parallel effectuation. Cryptographic causal dependency: Receipt-derived execution material, split credentials, tokenless continuation, hardware-gated enablement, and protected state transitions. Protected evidence semantics: Proof of delivery versus proof of effect, negative receipts, receipt freshness, destination binding, cross-device protection, Merkle receipt structures, and privacy-preserving confirmation. Independent continuation authority: Human, automatic, hybrid, and multi-authority decisions separated from the potentially compromised AI-agent environment. Fail-closed recovery: Missing or conflicting receipts, uncertain outcomes, replay protection, atomic consumption, reconciliation, and prevention of blind retries. Anti-bypass enforcement: Protected execution boundaries, credential surrogation, taint and provenance controls, alternative-path closure, and software–hardware implementation independence. A principal contribution is a catalogue of 146 numbered technical embodiments, organized into 19 groups, covering AI-agent tool execution, messages and file delivery, payments and settlement, data export, cloud and model deployment, databases, persistent model memory, GPUs and accelerators, robotics, industrial controllers, vehicles, UAVs, telecommunications, satellite systems, and distributed infrastructure. Illustrative workflows show how sensitive communications may release a limited verification object before the full payload; how a bounded payment authorization may precede settlement; how verified cloud canary results may gate broader deployment; and how measured physical movement may enable subsequent actuator authority. In each staged example, the initial effect is real—not merely simulated—and subsequent authority depends on protected validation of its observed result. The central research proposition is that evidence should not merely explain what happened after execution. For selected high-consequence operations, independently verified evidence should determine whether further execution is technically possible. The architecture does not require every operation to be staged. Protected policy may authorize single-phase execution where the consequence model permits it. Nor does validation of one phase guarantee that all later outcomes will be correct. The design instead establishes bounded, conditional progression under explicit trust and enforcement assumptions. This publication provides a technical architecture, formal relationships, execution workflows, and a catalogue of embodiments. It is a design and analytical contribution, not an experimentally validated implementation. Patent pending: The document identifies the related invention as “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” No conclusion concerning patentability, enforceable patent scope, infringement, or implementation by any particular commercial system is asserted. Invitation for independent technical validation: Frontier AI providers, security architects, researchers, hardware engineers, distributed-systems specialists, and critical-infrastructure operators are invited to examine the 146 embodiments, identify relevant prior art, evaluate the receipt-to-authority dependency, challenge the anti-bypass assumptions, and propose alternative implementations. Independent criticism, adversarial testing, and evidence-based technical conclusions are welcomed.

items.title: Evolution of Automatic Paper Electrocardiogram Digitization: Methods, Applications, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of global mortality, and the electrocardiogram (ECG) is among the most widely used diagnostic tools. However, a substantial number of ECG records remain available only as paper records or scanned images, which are susceptible to aging, fading, and other forms of physical degradation, leading to information loss. Automatic paper ECG digitization, which involves reconstructing machine-readable waveforms from visual records, offers an effective means of transforming historical ECG records into reusable digital data. This systematic review synthesizes the evolution of automatic paper ECG digitization following the PRISMA framework and analyzes 78 studies. We first summarize public ECG databases and emerging image-based datasets and then examine the digitization pipeline across three stages: image preprocessing, waveform localization and extraction, and signal calibration and reconstruction. Both traditional computer vision techniques and deep learning methods are systematically compared, highlighting a shift from handcrafted rules toward data-driven feature learning that improves robustness to noise, waveform overlap, and heterogeneous layouts. We further review major applications, including historical data recovery, automated diagnosis, monitor calibration, and multimodal digital health integration. Key challenges are identified, notably the scarcity of paired image–signal datasets, the absence of standardized evaluation protocols, limited interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation. Future progress will depend on standardized benchmarks, lightweight and interpretable models, and multimodal and foundation-model approaches to enable robust, generalizable, and clinically applicable ECG digitization. By transforming legacy paper and image-based ECG records into machine-readable signals, ECG digitization can also serve as an enabling technology for multimodal physiological signal processing and artificial intelligence-driven health monitoring, contributing to the broader digital health ecosystem.

items.abstract: Evolution of Capability Leadership opens the seven-part Capability Leadership Series by examining how leadership enables people, collective judgement, work systems and technology to deliver reliable, responsible and sustained organisational outcomes.Drawing on NASA’s documented approach to capability leadership, the paper develops a broader interpretation for the AI era. It proposes a definition of Capability Leadership and examines the conditions through which expertise can be applied, decisions acted upon and capability sustained as work changes.The discussion connects leadership responsibility with human judgement, human–AI collaboration, workplace learning and TechnoEthics. Practical workplace examples help leaders consider how authority, access to expertise, coordination, oversight and opportunities for learning affect the outcomes their organisations depend on.CLS-01 establishes the conceptual foundation for the series and invites leaders and practitioners to examine what must change for organisational capability to be developed, applied, trusted and sustained.

items.title: Examining the effect of work-life integration on burnout among Indonesian employees
items.abstract: Background: Burnout remains a critical occupational health issue in Indonesia. While previous studies often focus on static Work-Life Balance, modern workplace requires a dynamic Work-Life Integration (WLI) approach, yet dimensions mitigating burnout remain unclear.Purpose: This study investigates how WLI affects employee burnout and identifies specific dimensions acting as protective factors or stressors, alongside demographic boundary conditions.Method: A cross-sectional survey involved 355 employees (Mage = 32.08, SD = 10; 67.9% male and 32.1% female) across Western, Central, and Eastern Indonesia. Data were collected using the Maslach-Trisni Burnout Inventory (𝛼 = .916) and transadapted Work-Life Indicator Scale with internal consistency for WLI dimensions ranging from 𝛼 = .664 to .837. Regression and correlation analyses were conducted using SPSS and Multigroup Analysis (PLS-MGA) using SmartPLS.Findings: Multidimensional WLI predicts burnout (R2 = 17.6%). Work Identity (b = -.269) and Boundary Control (b = -.131) protect against burnout, whereas Non-Work Interrupting Work acts as a stressor. PLS-MGA reveals that Work Interrupting Non-work intensifies burnout specifically among permanent and single employees.Discussion: Professional identity and boundary management appear more critical than role fusion in preventing burnout, highlighting the need for targeted, demographic-sensitive boundary management addressing vulnerabilities related to employment status and marital demands.

items.title: Existing and emerging in vitro and in vivo methods for protein and amino acid assessment in foods: a systematic review of methodological advances, validation, and predictive performance
items.abstract: Protein and amino acid assessment is central to nutrition, food formulation and regulatory evaluation, particularly as novel and sustainable protein sources expand. This systematic review synthesizes 2016–2026 evidence on methods for protein quantity/quality, amino acid composition and digestibility, with emphasis on methodological comparison, validation and predictive performance. The evidence spans nitrogen-based methods, amino acid hydrolysis and chromatography, static and dynamic in vitro digestion, in vivo ileal digestibility, DIAAS and PDCAAS, spectroscopy, peptidomics, microfluidics and artificial intelligence (AI). Amino acid methods generally reported recoveries of approximately 90–105% and relative standard deviations (RSDs) below about 3–8%, whereas spectroscopy/AI studies commonly reported R2 values of approximately 0.85–0.99. Selected in vitro validation studies reported correlations above r = 0.8, but these were matrix-specific and did not establish agreement or absence of systematic bias; reported paired differences of approximately 5–15% between some in vitro and in vivo digestibility estimates likewise varied by matrix and protocol. These findings indicate that analytical accuracy, agreement with a reference method, biological validity and regulatory validity are distinct evidence domains. Persistent sources of uncertainty include matrix effects, non-protein nitrogen, incomplete or differential amino acid recovery, digestion-model assumptions, inter-laboratory variability, limited external validation of AI models, and incomplete translation of in vitro findings to human physiological utilization. The synthesis therefore supports a staged evidence framework in which chemical measurement feeds amino acid recovery, digestibility estimation and DIAAS calculation, followed by validation against physiological outcomes before methods are used for definitive nutritional or regulatory decisions.
